items.title: Now Is The Time For Hysteria
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
We had ourselves the hell week of all hell weeks last Saturday. And in the aftermath, the top of the sport is upside down and everyone sounds incoherent—babbling and whining about which teams are good and which are bad, in tones you can otherwise only find from Old Testament prophets. Is Florida secretly good? Is Texas truly a tire fire? Is it going to come out that Cooper Manning never even showed Arch a football before college? Why can't Notre Dame close? Why would Oregon bench Dylan Raiola, just to play him in the fourth quarter against his former school? How did we end up with a first-ranked Miami? These are the questions left to us in the wake of some near-unprecedented football mayhem. The two directions left to go from here are either set the universal order right or make shit go even more left. I know what I choose.

After the pyro-spectacular of last weekend, with all those ranked teams either losing outright or barely escaping defeat, something needed to be done to restore normalcy. And so Maryland fired head coach Mike Locksley on Tuesday. Locksley is most recently noted for having guided the Terps to 12 consecutive conference losses, seven of the last eight by double digits, and the most recent coming against Rutgers. The last and decisive one was just a seven-point loss, but it may as well have been 49 when you apply the added "You lost to RUTGERS?" metric.

items.title: James Dolan Finds Innovative New Way To Be Cruel And Cheap
items.author: Samer Kalaf
items.content:
Most owners of sports teams are wise enough to understand that their reputations will never be better than when their teams are winning. If they're fortunate enough to see that team capture a championship, they know that it's easy image rehabilitation. Just show some basic appreciation, sprinkle it around to everyone in the organization, and try not to say much aside from "We did it" and "Thank you." That way, the public will momentarily forget how you made your money off predatory mortgages or whatever.

James Dolan has chosen a different path. Since June, when the New York Knicks won their first title in 53 years, the owner has done his best to make the victory lap as unpleasant as possible for all involved. At the championship ceremony, in a juiceless and mercifully short speech, Dolan took swipes at New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and—for some reason—Knicks fans under the age of 53. He brought back notable creep Isiah Thomas, and appointed him to the team's board of directors. He scheduled a fundraiser for Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman right before a Knicks preseason game, and has sued magazine for reporting on the invasive surveillance technology he uses at Madison Square Garden. He's also played hardball in contract talks with the very stars who won a championship. It's rare to have a title-winning team begin its subsequent season on such a sour note.

But wait, there's more: According to Joe Vardon of The Athletic, the Knicks' pregame ceremony ahead of Tuesday's season opener was a bit more ceremonial than it appeared. Team president Leon Rose opened a box to show off his sparkly championship ring, but nobody on the coaching staff did, because their boxes were empty. They didn't have rings yet, and it was still unclear who would actually receive one. From the article:

items.title: How Can I Hang On To My Digital Life?
items.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
items.content:
I've been watching the "available storage" bars on my various digital storage systems creep up over the last couple years, with a growing sense of dread. Each percentage point is a tick closer to an upgrade to my package—money I'll have to pay Apple, Google, and Dropbox to continue to store my digital life. Maybe more importantly, I'm aware of just how much I produce every day, and as the mess grows, I wonder if I should do something about it. On worse days, I think maybe I should just succumb to the digital hoarder house I've built for myself.

It is probably my obsession with my own death, paired with the ever-present anxiety about whether the way I spend my days truly matters at all, that has led to an interest in personal archiving practices. My life's work amounts to several terabytes' worth of mp3s, wavs, text files, and jpegs that live on server space I pay to lease somewhere in the world. I like the idea of my work being accessible after I'm gone, and for a long time I trusted the infrastructure of the internet to do that archival work for me. But if the last 20 years have taught us anything, it's that only dummies blindly trust big tech to operate in their best interest.

items.title: Catapult Elizabeth Koch Into The Sun
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
I don't know if Elizabeth Koch would fashion herself a personal essayist, but she has certainly dabbled in the form. In an 11-part essay published in in 2007, the billionaire's daughter who describes herself as "apolitical" wrote about a trip she took to Japan with her boyfriend at the time, Todd. The essay opens with her and Todd buying candy-flavored drinks from a vending machine. They buy eight, take a sip from each, and then discard them on top of a mailbox, where Koch includes the following exchange.

"Just line them up on top of the machine," I say. "Maybe a homeless person will find them."

We look around. No sign of a homeless person.

"What do you think they do with their homeless people here?"

"They probably hide them wherever they hide the trash," Todd says. I laugh, and try to take his arm, but he rips it away from me.

It is probably unsurprising that this is what Koch presumes passes for affectionate banter between her and Todd. Much of the essay appears to be a direct transcript between Koch and Todd, in which she quotes him saying "It's just up here" and "Huh." The two get into a fight after Koch buys Todd an expensive pair of headphones—a reminder to both of her unfathomable net worth—after which Todd walks away. Koch then wanders the streets and sees two Japanese people with albinism. "Their skin is pinkish and their hair is white and their bodies are lumpy, and I wonder what it would be like to be stripped of tone and color in a city where most everyone looks the same," Koch writes, before deciding to photograph the people—the photo appears in the body of the essay—so that she and Todd can talk about them later. She laments her privilege and its terrible, burdensome baggage. "I'm angry that those girls on the playground in sixth grade called me a rich bitch when they knew nothing about me except my last name," Koch writes, patently unaware that she is proving their thesis correct.

items.title: The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off Fails To Rise For Bread Week
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off, where Kelsey and Chris attempt to complete the technical challenges from the newest season of The Great British Bake Off in their own home kitchens, with the same time parameters as the professional-grade bakers competing on the show.This week, Kelsey was unable to participate in the challenge, due to scheduling.

Bread Week never quite delivers. It's annoying, because bread-making is the quintessence of baking, and bread is considered by historians and whatnot to be one of humankind's very oldest prepared foods. A baking challenge that did not give proper space for straightforward bread-making would be, in a word, baloney. Also it just kicks ass to make a good loaf of bread, it's a proud accomplishment. A good homemade loaf of bread increases your Human Heritage score by one unit. You can reach into the past and link hands with the ancients by tying a good knot, or fashioning a clean dovetail joint, sure, but you cannot eat those things, and they do not smell good in your kitchen. Bake bread.

items.title: The U.S.-Funded Plan To Kill Infants In Africa By Withholding Vaccines Has Been Thwarted
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
This week, one of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s most malevolent plots was finally brought to a halt when police in Guinea-Bissau raided the offices of Danish researchers who intended to carry out a hepatitis B vaccine trial that would have endangered thousands of newborn children in Africa and condemned some of them to an early, agonizing death. The trial was to be funded with $1.6 million from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

This hopefully marks the end one of the most unethical research projects proposed in recent memory. (There is, by the way, some stiff competition there, what with the National Institute of Justice's recent announcement that it will fund $1 million in research into possible links between "gender dysphoria and violent crime.") If you had not heard of the Guinea-Bissau trial until now, you might be thinking, well, why do I need to know about a shitty trial that is now cancelled? To that I would say: It's important to pay attention to the kind of straightforwardly evil machinations RFK Jr. is trying to pull off to advance his anti-vaccine agenda, because he's very likely going to try to do something like this again.

A huge part of the reason the Guinea-Bissau trial has flown largely under the radar—with the notable exception of ongoing coverage at and —is because it would take place in Africa and on African children, a population that, despite not living in the U.S., has already become a casualty of our stupid and monstrous government doing stupid and monstrous things with our tax dollars. So anyway, here's what happened. Sorry it is so long. It is intricately evil.

items.title: Martin Mull Was A Good Painter And A Great Documentary Subject
items.author: Brandy Jensen
items.content:
As a culture, we have a few familiar stories about talent. There’s the all-consuming kind, often first displayed in childhood, that makes people unsuited for the demands of everyday life. There are the stories about talent that goes tragically unrecognized until after a person has died. Alternatively, there’s the sort of talent that falls just short of greatness. Think Salieri, or that guy you work with who played sports in college.

Martin Mull’s story is different. He had prodigious talents—as a musician, a stand-up comedian, an actor—and they were widely recognized throughout his long career. In 1970 he wrote the hit novelty song “A Girl Named Johnny Cash,” a parody of Cash's "A Boy Named Sue," then spent most of that decade touring his stand-up show regularly and successfully. He opened for Bruce Springsteen and Billy Joel, and was tapped by none other than TV icon Norman Lear to star in the mock talk show . Mull also guest-hosted for Johnny Carson more than 30 times. He became, through performances in a variety of films and television shows spanning decades, a guy you were always excited to see in a scene. He had one of those faces it felt like you’ve always known, whether it was as Colonel Mustard or Gene Parmesan. Through all of that, though, the one thing Mull really wanted to be known for was his painting.

items.title: The Connor Hellebuyck Showdown Is About To Get Expensive For The Jets
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Connor Hellebuyck goes back on the Winnipeg Jets payroll today, which must come as a great source of joy and satisfaction to ... well, who, exactly?

Hellebuyck is, as you may remember from that burst of not-entirely-misguided patriotism you felt back in February during the Winter Olympics, the goalie for the gold medal–winning U.S. men's hockey team. He is also the longtime goalie of the Winnipeg Jets, kind of, and by acclaim the finest practitioner of that extremely difficult job on earth. Well, until lately.

items.title: These WNBA Finals Are Made Of Steal
items.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
items.content:
The shooting gods may be weeping, but these WNBA Finals are a steal lover's delight. Jordin Canada, at 5-foot-6, shoots the gap and sneaks behind the unsuspecting. Angel Reese, who can time up a dribble better than anyone, favors the on-ball poke-away to punish players foolish enough to try to cross her over. Against would-be kickouts and outlets, Rhyne Howard makes plays you might see from a defensive back in zone coverage. She’s locked in on the quarterback’s eyes before she jumps the route and picks off the pass. 

Steals have swung the possession game for the Atlanta Dream in these playoffs, and so far have swung series for them, too. They came away with 16 steals to open the first round against the Washington Mystics and followed those up with another 10 in Game 2. Across three games against the veteran New York Liberty in the semifinals, the Dream logged another 26. And after only having five steals to show for their efforts in Game 1 of the Finals, Atlanta’s first loss of the postseason, the Dream seem to have regained their penchant for pilfering on the way to taking a 2-1 series lead. The Golden State Valkyries were on the wrong end of 14 steals in Game 2 and nine in Game 3. “We always say, ‘thieves in the night,’” a smiling Reese told me the day before Game 1. She said her teammate Allisha Gray has another saying: “We’ll steal the drawers off you.”

items.title: Here Comes The Fun Part
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Like a tuna fish sandwich, quaint has a shelf life. Also like a tuna fish sandwich, it's definitely shorter than four days. All the charms of two teams meeting in the World Series that have never won a championship before have played themselves out in the time between the last playoff game and the next one. The amusements that come with two lower-half payrolls making baseball's radicalized reigning billionaires look like the amoral sludge smugglers they are are pretty much done, too. To put it as simply as possible, our culture doesn't have four days of anticipation in it before boredom starts to creep into emotional ennui. Replacing all that abstracted fussing with some actual baseball is a good deal for all involved.

The World Series starts tonight, and the field has been cleared of distractions. The Tampa Bay "Once Again" Devil Rays and Milwaukee "Used To Be Seattle Pilots" Brewers are now down to work, and those games will constitute a final plebiscite on How To Play The Game. The Rays and Brewers have made use of defense and speed and even bunting in ways that have lately fallen out of fashion. It's as if they found a dusty box in the attic with some ominous scrolls in it, but so far the incantations have worked like a dream. They are thin on power but generate plenty of runs; they both are pitching-rich, and make deft and still slightly unconventional use of the when-in-doubt-use-an-opener maneuver that dominates postseason baseball.

In other words, they will give the baseball public all the things it says it wants: movement, dexterity, the art of the game, pitching changes and discussions about pitching changes, not being the Dodgers or the Mets or any of the other high-payroll teams, and also not being the teams that don't try and don't want to. The element of novelty is all well and good, and the styles-make-fights aspect of the matchup suggests that these games will also offer something for the purists and true heads. If you're lucky, Pat Murphy might say something pithier than "Goddamnit, Merrill," and a Junior Caminero home run moonwalk might take three minutes. Now the issue becomes whether that—crackerjack baseball played by people whose names even most casual fans might not know—is actually what you want. That, ultimately, is between you and your landlord.

items.title: Brian Evenson Will Mess With Your Head
items.author: Adam Fleming Petty
items.content:
Brian Evenson’s first book, a story collection titled came out in 1994. It was not widely reviewed. The few notices the book did receive in the media ranged from the curious, to the baffled, to the outright disturbed. “In a capsule review, the nervously conceded that ‘there is a talent here,’ albeit, ‘an eldritch one,’” noted Ben Ehrenreich in an essay about Evenson’s work that appeared in One reviewer, though, an anonymous one, was unequivocal in their dismay over the book’s violent content, which included dismemberment, mutilation, insects placed in the mouths of corpses, and defenestration, among other indignities. “I feel like someone who has eaten something poisonous and is desperate to get rid of it,” wrote the nameless critic. 

This particular review would prove enormously consequential for Evenson’s career—indeed, for his life. It did not appear in a journal or a newspaper. It was not even published, technically. Rather, it was sent to Evenson’s employer, a university, triggering an inquiry that would lead to his dismissal. 

The nameless critic was a student at Brigham Young University, the flagship institution of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, located in Provo, Utah, where Evenson taught for the good reason that he was a devout Mormon, raised in the faith his whole life. The student wrote to the university out of concern that a violent, disturbing book like was not the sort of literary work that good Mormon professors should be pursuing. Over the course of the long and involved inquiry process, Evenson was presented with a choice. If he wished to continue working at BYU, he would have to stop writing books like that. If he didn’t stop, he would have to leave.

items.title: A Cool Night
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season. Got something you wanna contribute? . You can also read Drew over at

I have another soccer game to attend. This has been a parental duty for me and my wife ever since our son got into the sport sometime around the age of zero. You have kids, and you soon realize that the bulk of your time will be spent driving them places. As such, my wife and I have spent the past 17 years driving our son to soccer practice, soccer meetings, soccer games, and soccer team pizza parties. We’ve done this without malice, but the practice can’t help but turn a bit rote when you’ve been doing it for as long as we have.

That’s been especially true during the boy’s senior year of high school. This year, he finally made the varsity team. No small accomplishment, but one that requires a great deal of his time and, by association, ours. Practices every day. Two games a week, some of them on the road, all of them extending relatively late into the evening. At one point, his team played a streak of half a dozen games that went to extra time; many of these were played in the rain, which I found extra rude. Some nights, he’s had to do his homework after coming back late from these games. Thus, the schedule is so demanding that the games, for any parent, can begin to feel like a bit of obligation.

items.title: Defector’s Completely Decentralized NBA Season Preview Has Now Been Recentralized
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
Defector will publish no written league-wide preview for the 2026-27 NBA season. Not even a cute, belatedly published one, either. Instead we enlisted Harry Krinsky, co-host of our podcast and avant-garde vertical video artist, to preview each team. He then produced mankind's first completely decentralized NBA season preview, which has been recentralized for your viewing pleasure below. Here's Harry:

They said it couldn’t be done. They said nobody could create a completely decentralized NBA season preview by way of 30 morsels of short-form video content. Well, they were wrong. With help from the good people of Defector, I have made 30 strange videos, one for every NBA team, previewing the upcoming NBA season. They are now all live in four places: the Defector Instagram, the Defector YouTube, my Twitter feed, and my TikTok page.

Check them out on the platform of your choice, and tune in to this week’s to hear me and Patrick Redford talk a little bit about what it was like making them. Below are a few images that made their way into some of the videos, to give you a sense of what I was going for.

items.title: Basketball Game Interrupts Shit-Talk Session Between Luka Doncic And Yaxel Lendeborg
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
For months, I've seen Michigan basketball fans chortle ominously about the big personality of Yaxel Lendeborg, the super-senior who led the Wolverines' 2026 national championship run then sidled over to the NBA draft, where he was selected at No. 11 by the Golden State Warriors. They'd murmur something about him being blunt, being goofy, the world isn't ready for him, etc. Sure.

I knew the backstory: Born to parents who had both played basketball for the Dominican Republic's national teams, Lendeborg barely participated in organized basketball for most of his schooling because he couldn't keep his grades up, preferring instead to play video games all day, and had no intention to play college ball until pushed by his mom to play in a showcase for Dominican players at the end of high school. His highlights there won him the last scholarship slot at Arizona Western College, and after a cumulative six seasons of college hoops, a first-round NBA draft selection, a Summer League MVP, and a strong preseason, he started at power forward in his NBA debut on Wednesday. A remarkable sequence of events.

The Warriors targeted 24-year-old Lendeborg rather than taking a younger prospect, presumably because they wanted a fresh-out-of-the-box starter to retain a competitive team around Steph Curry. It's a noble thought, but at least one game in, with Jimmy Butler still months away from a return after ACL repair, and Kristaps Porzingis reportedly considering retirement due to chronic illness, the Warriors look dismal. While they were getting shredded by the Los Angeles Lakers, 127-105, Lendeborg exchanged lots of animated words and gestures with inveterate shit-talker Luka Doncic. Just before the halftime buzzer, Doncic banked in a half-court shot over Lendeborg, and the two resumed barking at each other.

items.title: It’s Hard To Be A Rich Radical
items.author: Israel Daramola
items.content:
, a column where I share the music and musical topics I’ve been fixated on recently.

What could compel someone to spend four hours on a YouTube essay mostly about the rapper Killer Mike, a B-tier Dungeon Family affiliate who parlayed success as one half of Run The Jewels to become a B-tier rap A-lister? In truth, it is no worse than sitting through six hours of self-assigned Super Bowl performer Jay-Z and Rick Rubin yap about rap and also therapy. Or watching a three-hour documentary on disgraced Silicon Valley fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in a hilariously, extremely sold-out theater. Or watching four hours of Nick Saban coaching propaganda. Or one hour of an ESPN soft-focus profile of Ben Simmons that tries to sidestep the question of Simmons’ work ethic. I watch a lot of nonsense, I guess it’s safe to say—and people are apparently greatly long-winded.

Maybe a better question is: Who would actually be compelled to a four-hour YouTube video on Killer Mike? For that answer, we’d have to get into who FD Signifier and Jared A. Ball are, and the importance of the latter’s book, . Then we would have to talk about black leftist politics and anticapitalist critique and how exactly we got to a point where a bunch of people think Killer Mike is at war with black activist streamers and content creators, and shooting at them in random freestyles.

items.title: Vivek Ramaswamy Is Going After The Abusive Parent Vote
items.author: David Roth
items.content:
This is not to discredit the existence of some underlying tactical or strategic calculations, and it is absolutely not extending credit to the shockingly vile creatures doing it, but when you see a reactionary candidate being disgusting, it is safe to assume that they are doing it because they really believe in it. The decade and change in which Donald Trump has been the main character in American public life has been a notably bad one for metaphor and subtext, among other things, but it has been a notably revealing one where some fundamental national political impulses are concerned. Trump himself is too dim and too brazen for that game's familiar euphemisms, and his inability or unwillingness to promise to deliver harm in the usual coded language was central to his political appeal. It was also novel enough to convince some people that he was interested in doing something other than inflicting that pain.

This was true for partisans who thrilled at hearing him make explicit the implicit conservative value of hurting the most vulnerable people, and also to a significant faction of people without any other real values who mistook the brutal liberties that Trump has always taken for himself for ones that they would be able to enjoy themselves by supporting him. There is no other way to say it: Donald Trump these people. He inspired them to be their worst and smallest and cruelest selves, but inspiration is a value-neutral thing. This is to say that he inspired those people to be more like him, and to live as he lives—in the indulgent certainty that even their puniest comfort or fleeting amusement or flash of childish anger was more important than anything or anyone else in the world, and then to behave accordingly. Many of these people surely had suspected as much already and moved through the world as if it were true; the carnage and stupid suffering that all that heedless, headlong motion produces is everywhere you look. Some of these people, inevitably, were going to run for political office.

People like that will always be a danger to everyone around them, but it's at this point that they truly become everyone's problem. There is a world in which Vivek Ramaswamy is just one of the many millions of Americans—please do not think about how many there are, how many you have met and will someday meet—who just are , and move through their days with what even a layperson could diagnose as "walking malignant narcissism." But that alternate-universe Ramaswamy would be contained within some grim gated community and grim gated personal and business relationships; his capacity to do the damage such a person would invariably do would be limited to those unfortunate enough to wind up in his path. That Ramaswamy would also be an extremely odious man, a curdled being driven entirely by resentment and appetite. But very few people would ever know his name. That's the best-case scenario.

items.title: Aaron Sorkin Wants To Pretend The Good Guys Won
items.author: Imran Zaidi
items.content:
In 2000, midway through the first season of , Aaron Sorkin started posting on a discussion forum on the site Television Without Pity as “Benjamin,” his middle name. Specifically, he posted on the forum dedicated to discussing . “Benjamin” was met with some initial skepticism, but after proving to their satisfaction that he really was the show’s creator, his interactions with fans were warm. They fawned over him, and he thanked them for watching. Things took a turn in 2001 when posters commented on Sorkin’s unseemly hogging of the mic in an acceptance speech for an Emmy he won with a co-writer, Rick Cleveland. The incident snowballed into full-fledged forum drama, with Sorkin and Cleveland trading lengthy, bitter replies; Sorkin eventually admitted he was wrong, apologized, and stopped posting. Later, when the site’s recaps took a more critical turn, he reappeared, angry and defensive, asking why the recapper was even bothering to watch the show and write about it if she didn’t like it. The site’s founder responded that the recapper was doing this because it was her job and they paid her.

This was Sorkin’s first dance with the internet, and it seems to have left a mark. An entire storyline in a third-season episode is dedicated to White House deputy chief of staff Josh Lyman discovering a Josh Lyman fan forum and accidentally running afoul of its hostile, pajama-clad users. The forum’s moderator, who polices infractions like posting in the wrong thread or writing in all caps, is described by Josh as “a dictatorial leader who I’m sure wears a muumuu and chain-smokes Parliaments.” Sorkin’s next TV show, Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip, careened between goofy comedy and somber drama as it struggled and ultimately failed to find its footing, but a consistent thread was the corrosive influence of the internet, manifested in everything from unscrupulous gossip bloggers to foreign terrorists posting hostage videos on YouTube. was similarly erratic in tone while even more laser-focused on the harm that the likes of Gawker and Twitter were causing to journalism, politics, and our very souls. In its unapologetically pro-elite credentialism, its score-settling attitude toward women, and its often deranged determination to offer Frank Capra-style uplift no matter the circumstances, the show remains the purest distillation of Sorkin’s fixations.

In 2010, when was released, the general public largely still trusted the tech industry. The iPhone felt futuristic. Facebook was still kind of cool. Today, depicting Silicon Valley as a malign force is cliché; 16 years ago, it was subversive. The alchemy of Sorkin’s collaboration with David Fincher—a non-obvious director for a quippy, dense script—resulted in a perfectly calibrated dark comedy warning us about the future of human interaction and the people bringing it into being. In the decade that followed, reality caught up to the film’s bleak outlook. The preoccupations that had once marked Sorkin as an aggrieved and out-of-touch Luddite now made him look improbably prescient. It makes sense that he would feel the urge to take a victory lap.

items.title: Ottawa Vs. Brady Tkachuk Was Fantastic Theater
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
There's a type of hate that's easy to love. It's the hate a downtrodden fanbase feels for a homegrown star who forced his way out, to a better or at least more glamorous situation. This hate is full and rich and multifaceted. It contains all the frustrations of decades of losing, of free agents spurning their team as a destination, of being a punchline for the rest of the league. It contains envy and resentment toward the idea that someone could just choose not to live or die with the fortunes of that benighted franchise. It contains disappointment in that departed star, for getting their hopes up and leaving them dangling. It contains a heart-tugging exasperation that gets deep into sports' very real ability to encapsulate the human condition: it says. Not since Long Island "welcomed" back John Tavares has there been a night of hockey hate like Brady Tkachuk's return to Ottawa on Wednesday. He may be Keith Tkachuk's garbage son, but for eight years he was Ottawa's garbage son, too, dammit.

Ottawa's easy to root for from afar. They've dealt with more shit than any fanbase should be expected to. They weathered an evil and stupid owner, and threats of relocation. They've been the butt of the joke on the ice, failing to win a playoff series in the last decade and reaching one Final in their entire existence. Everyone dumps on their town, even, accidentally, their own mayor. Players don't want to live there. If they are to have their very own superstar, they have to make one. For the Senators' drawn-out trek into and then gradually out of the wilderness, that was Brady Tkachuk.

Tkachuk makes a great bad guy. He already has the bearing and showmanship of a pro-wrestling heel, and the way he forced his way to Florida was genuinely villainous: quietly, on the mythical Team USA group chat, and publicly, on his podcast with his father and brother. (Tampering is an unenforceable rule, but it's to not even try to pretend to follow it.) He's an avatar for the U.S.'s aggressive geopolitical little-brothering of Canada. He's unlikable as a person and infuriating as an opposing player. He is very fun to boo, and he is of the temperament to enjoy being booed.

items.title: The Dream Are Making Bully Ball Literal
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
There's a sequence from the first quarter of Game 3 of the WNBA Finals, in which the Atlanta Dream walloped the Golden State Valkyries by a score of 97-71, that would still be grinding my gears if I were a Valks fan. Angel Reese, fresh off her Game 2 masterpiece, started Game 3 aggressively, going right to the rim. She scored the first two points of the game on a nifty duck-in, and then tried to drive on Kiah Stokes on two straight possessions. Stokes blocked her both times, and then blocked a Jordin Canada layup. And then, with just over five minutes left in the quarter, Stokes was subbed out of the game.

One of the most noticeable subplots of these Finals is what Reese is able to do when Stokes is and is not matched up with her. When defended by Stokes, she has sometimes struggled to reliably get off clean shots; against every other big on the Valks' roster, she has enjoyed a feast of layups and fouls. Things were no different on Wednesday night: As soon as Aminata Gueye subbed in for Stokes in the first quarter, Reese went straight at her for a bucket and a foul. When Stokes was subbed out again with 7:23 left in the second quarter, Reese got right back to work by hitting a three in Gueye's face and then bumping her out of the way for another layup.

The Valkyries and Dream are stylistically similar in a number of meaningful ways, but one area where they diverge is their depth. Golden State has ridden its 10-player rotation to the Finals by believing in every player's ability to contribute, and by prioritizing meaningful amounts of in-game rest for the starters. The Dream, meanwhile, are happy to share minutes among just seven players. A deep roster full of talented players is the kind of thing that can help carry a team through the regular season and a long playoff run, but a dogmatic commitment to using a big rotation can make it harder to navigate that other all-important principle of playoff basketball: matchups.

items.title: BioWare Becomes First Major Casualty Of Saudi Arabia’s EA Takeover
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content: When news came out that Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund had taken a majority stake in Electronic Arts last September, it was clear to anyone familiar with Saudi Arabia, EA, private equity, or capitalism that the move would make an already terrible gaming company even worse. I wrote as much at the time, and though the sale took until August of this year to go through, I can grimly say that I was completely right: On Wednesday, video game reporter Jason Schreier reported that EA had shut down BioWare, the game studio behind classic role-playing game series such as , Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and .

items.title: Robert Saleh Says Jordan Elliott Needs Help, Not Condemnation
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
Tennessee Titans defensive tackle Jordan Elliott was a surprise inactive for Sunday's game, not traveling with the team. Head coach Robert Saleh told reporters only that Elliott was "dealing with personal stuff." On Tuesday, the Titans released Elliott, along with a cryptic statement referencing an "incident." One never wants to have an incident, but the lack of detail only made the whole thing more mysterious.

Elliott and offensive tackle JC Latham got into a fight during drills at the Titans' facility, the reports say, and Elliott was told by coaches to leave the field. He left the building, going out to the players' parking lot with the intention of retrieving a gun from his car. Defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers, a real hero here, was able to talk Elliott out of getting the gun, and he never brought it back into the building.

items.title: ‘Digger’ Is Smug, Cynical, And Perfectly Timed
items.author: Osita Nwanevu
items.content:
On the night of May 10, 1968, the most storied night in the last century of French civil unrest, nearly 40,000 students faced off against policemen in the Latin Quarter of Paris—one of the largest crowds the city's swelling protest movement had yet assembled. Famously, cobblestones were torn up from the streets to erect barricades. By the time morning broke, hundreds of demonstrators had been beaten bloody or arrested anyway. That same evening, the Cannes Film Festival opened with a ceremony hosted by retired actress Grace Kelly, Princess of Monaco, and a screening of a restored edition of .

That juxtaposition quickly led to calls for the festival’s suspension. On May 18, after a week of resistance from Cannes’s organizers, a group of filmmakers and guests led by the directors Francois Truffaut and Jean-Luc Godard held a press conference demanding a closure. “There isn’t one film showing the problems going on today among workers and students⁠—not one, whether by Forman, myself, Polanski, or Francois,” Godard said. “There are none. We’re behind the times. Our student comrades set an example by getting their heads bashed in last week.” 

There were grumbles in the crowd at this, and Godard’s patience snapped. “We’re talking solidarity with students and workers, and you’re talking dolly shots and close-ups!” he yelled. “You’re assholes!”

items.title: How Do I Stop My Kid From Crashing Out Over Trying New Activities?
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content: This week, Ray answers a question on how to deal with your child's tantrums over trying new activities.

items.title: A Review Of All The Stuff That Happened Last NBA Season
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content: On this week's episode of , the discerning listener can hear me and Harry, both of whom are recovering from minor illnesses, losing our voices over the course of an hour and a half. We had a lot to talk about, including the fact that we finally played basketball together, the ongoing WNBA Finals, Michael Porter Jr.'s podcasting habits, and, finally, the main event: a recap of the 2025-26 NBA season, from its inception through to the start of this current season. The logic here is that so much stuff happens in an NBA season that the best way to preview an upcoming season isn't to make predictions, but to lay out the historical record.

items.title: How Much Fire Emblem Is Too Much Fire Emblem?
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
When I was on the fence about buying a Nintendo Switch 2, I held off with the self-aware knowledge that I would eventually cave come September. I knew that Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave would break me. I needed to play this game like my life depended on it.

A month (and a few days) after release, I have 70-plus hours played on , and I wish it were double the amount. Still, 70 hours is a huge amount; aside from , I simply don't spend 70 hours on a single video game anymore. (The last "long" game I played was another strategy role-playing game, but even the remake only took me 36 hours to complete.) Fire Emblem is different, though. More than perhaps any video game series I have devoted chunks of my life to, Fire Emblem finds its way into both my waking thoughts and my sleeping nightmares. I began to see spreadsheets in the dark, thinking about ways to best build my virtual army of adorable murderers. I sought out the magic lightning Levin Swords in my deepest fantasies; words like "troubadour" and maybe-not-words like "bardinger" took on new meaning. I became obsessed, as fellow Defectorite Kathryn Xu could prove by producing even a portion of the many messages I have sent her about this game in just over a month.

items.title: How The Rams Being 2-4 Relates To The Troy Aikman Saga
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
In case you didn’t read about it, or you didn’t hear the hints firsthand, Joe Buck and Troy Aikman are reportedly getting divorced. The broadcast team is the longest-tenured booth duo in NFL history, even moving together from Fox to ESPN as a package deal four years ago. But Buck re-upped with the four-letter for a mint earlier this year, while Aikman, whose contract expires at the end of this season, was left to dangle. This perhaps represented the first time in history that Aikman did not say, “I completely agree with you, Joe,” to his longtime colleague. In fact, the men reportedly almost came to blows over Buck’s supposed betrayal. JUICY!

Believe those reports if you like (I do), but either way, Aikman has already openly talked about his “next landing spot,” which means there’s gonna be a big fat vacancy in the booth for ESPN to fill come this spring. What does that have to do with the Rams being the biggest disappointment in football? THAT, dear friends, is one of the Big Questions that Arif Hasan and I tackle on this week’s episode of

items.title: Nobody Wants To Talk About Why The Ringer Is Pivoting To Substack
items.author: Owen Lewis
items.content:
A media company launching a series of paywalled newsletters is not, on its own and on its face, a strange thing to do. AI’s ongoing cannibalization of online search is ravaging website traffic, and programmatic advertising doesn’t provide the kind of revenue it used to. If you were running a website like The Ringer, you might decide that it makes financial sense to put writing from some of your most popular staffers behind a paywall. That's exactly what has happened: Sean Fennessey, Zach Lowe, Tom Pelissero, and Bryan Curtis have all recently launched newsletters, only one of which (Curtis’s) is free. This seemingly normal business decision comes with a quirk, though, which is that the newsletters are being published on Substack. Nobody at The Ringer, or Substack, will tell you why.

This odd arrangement naturally raises a few questions: Why not just publish these writers’ work on The Ringer’s existing website? Does Spotify, which has owned The Ringer since 2020, somehow not have the technical capability to build its own paywall? If all of this valuable writing is going to live on an entirely different platform, what does that mean for the future of The Ringer’s editorial operation? Have the executives in charge of The Ringer, like seemingly everyone else, surrendered to the idea that Substack is the only place where people will actually read things anymore?

I emailed a few questions along these lines to Fennessey, a founder and executive at The Ringer, and more general questions to Lowe, Curtis, and Pelissero. None of them replied. I also reached out to Substack and Spotify, figuring that if the two companies had agreed on some sort of arrangement to produce these newsletters, their respective comms departments would be eager to trumpet their synergistic disruption of the publishing space. Neither company replied. It took reaching out to Ringer editor-in-chief Ben Glicksman to receive something resembling an official response. That came from Mallory Morehead Pritzl, part of the PR team for Spotify: "Thanks for reaching out. We are not commenting at this time."

items.title: The Pelicans Broke How I Understand Pro Basketball
items.author: Corban Goble
items.content:
It's unlikely that you spend much time thinking about the New Orleans Pelicans. However, as a New Orleans resident for whom ball is life, I am rather fixated on them. This team is far stranger than you may have previously understood. They suck in a singular way, and I’ve convinced myself to love them for it. No one else is doing it quite like this.

Any attention that was paid to the Pelicans by the broader NBA community last season was a result of one of the strangest trades in NBA history. This, you probably are familiar with: During the 2025 NBA draft, freshly installed Pelicans executives Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver traded an unprotected 2026 first-round pick in order to move up 10 slots and take Derik Queen at No. 13. The Pels have picked Queen at No. 7, which would have aligned with the organization’s internal valuation of him, but instead they decided to give up an extremely valuable future pick for a smiley, versatile big man who absolutely cannot play defense. The pick they gave up became a top-three selection for the Indiana Pacers in a consensus three-player draft in 2026, but thanks to some ping-pong balls, it instead became the eighth pick and remained with the Atlanta Hawks. So who’s laughing now? 

The Weaver-Dumars partnership is a particularly thrilling thread of this team’s current construction. Dumars—who last held an operations job for an NBA franchise in 2020, when he performed several jobs for the Sacramento Kings—worked at the NBA’s league office in Secaucus until the Pelicans hired him in 2025. In Detroit, where he last held a GM role, he flamed out spectacularly. Weaver also previously held the GM job in Detroit, and while he and Dumars never worked together, they arrived together in New Orleans as a kind of package deal. As GM of the Pistons from 2020-24, Weaver built rosters that compiled a 74-244 record. On his podcast, John Hollinger has called Weaver a “subcontractor” in the Pels' GM job, effectively just being the right arm of Dumars.

items.title: The Guardians Were And Are A Drag
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
The Cleveland Guardians will not win the World Series this autumn, just as they have not in any of the last 78 autumns. They were eliminated Monday night by the Tampa Bay Rays: outslugged, out-small-balled, and outlasted. Thus ends what was, by regular-season record, an uneven and dreary but still somehow typical year for the Guardians, who have won between 46 percent and 63 percent of their games every season for 14 years running. In terms of proximity to a championship, this was the most successful Guardians season since 2016, when they made the World Series and fell in seven games to the Chicago Cubs.

"We won another division," said a gloomy Austin Hedges after his Guardians were eliminated Monday night. "That's really cool. We won a playoff series. That's really cool." Hedges was hurting, and his point was that the objective coolness of these accomplishments would eventually penetrate his disappointment and give him a sense of satisfaction.

Unfortunately for Hedges, almost nothing about the Guardians can be honestly described as "cool." In the realm of aesthetics and vibes, let me say this much: I am glad I do not have to watch any more Guardians games between now and next summer. It's not that I bear them any specific ill will: Unlike at least one of my Defector colleagues, I am not pursuing an active personal vendetta against Steven Kwan. But as the Rays ascended in this ALCS—and as a consequence of the particular way that they ascended, by being better than the Guardians both where the Guardians are weak (hitting the ball hard, hitting the ball in the air) and where the Guardians are strong (posting crooked numbers without ever making solid contact)—they began to exude what I think of as the good kind of inevitability. Tampa Bay's guys were cool and cocky, they seemed downright saturated with juice, and at regular intervals they did bitchin' things. They seemed dialed to the moment, which is to say like a team that belonged in the World Series.

items.title: Mana Shim Walked Away From Soccer, Then She Rebuilt Her Life
items.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
items.content:
Five years ago this fall, The Athletic published a feature in which NWSL players Mana Shim and Sinead Farrelly opened up about their abusive former Portland Thorns coach, Paul Riley. The story prompted an investigation into how the NWSL handled reports of abuse, and by the end of that year, half of the league's head coaches either resigned or were fired, along with league commissioner Lisa Baird.

I met Shim while on tour for in 2023, and I was curious to talk to her about how she made the decision to go public with her experiences when there are so many reasons not to, like the fragility of the then-nascent league and the potential repercussions she might experience. And there were the identity questions. She had dedicated her entire life to soccer, so what happened when she decided to walk away? How did she find her way back on new terms after everything that had happened?

This season finale of is a bit heavier than the other episodes this season, but I wanted to end on it because I was so inspired by Shim's courage, not only to make herself vulnerable by speaking up, but in daring to imagine a new version of her life after spending so many years chasing a singular goal.

items.title: Angel Reese Crafted Her Masterpiece
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
Like its sludgy predecessor and by design, Game 2 of the WNBA Finals was played as if in the mud. Clean dribbling of the ball was prohibited, the two participants collaborated on 33 turnovers, and the Atlanta Dream finished one missed three-pointer beyond joining the Golden State Valkyries with an identical, gross 21-for-61 shooting night. Ballhalla's famous resolve was tested, as its stars spent the night dribbling sideways for 23 seconds before hoisting terrible shots. But through it all, directly in the middle of the fray on both ends of the court, there was one player who gradually revealed herself to be the game's protagonist, the one gleefully forcing the Valks down into the mud. There was Angel Reese, dominating the biggest game of her career and seizing control of the WNBA Finals for her team.

The stats tell some of the story: Reese finished with 30 points, 16 rebounds, and two blocks, got to the line 11 times, and finished as the only Atlanta player who made at least half their shot attempts. But the way her dominance was felt in the building was truly remarkable. Reese may as well have been the only player on the court. The San Francisco crowd puts a little extra energy into booing Reese, not out of a sense of culture-war conscription the way, say, an Indiana crowd would, but rather because she causes them the most pain.

Both these Finals teams are set up with the primary objective of preventing opponents from playing basketball, which played out for everyone in Game 1 and for the Valkyries in Game 2. Reese was the one player who was getting anything easy: If she got a touch with momentum or against anyone who wasn't Kiah Stokes, she was getting to the rim. If she pulled down an offensive rebound, the Valks may as well have started setting up their offense at the other end. In a series otherwise entirely populated with people moving sideways, Reese is direct. When she's on the court, she demands attention.

items.title: Polymarket Was Allowing Bets On Sexual Assault Cases Until People Started Asking Questions
items.author: Diana Moskovitz
items.content:
For nearly three weeks, a real bet a person could place on the Polymarket gambling app was on "Any of the Cornell 7 charged with a felony sex crime?" The Cornell 7 refers to seven defendants in a civil lawsuit filed last month by a former Cornell University student who said she was gang-raped by several fraternity members.

No criminal charges have been filed, but after the lawsuit drew national attention, a local prosecutor said on Sept. 28 that his office would reopen the criminal investigation. Two days later, on Sept. 30, a market opened up on the popular gambling platform (though technically it is a "prediction market") to bet on the results of the investigation. The market was not available to bettors in the United States version of the app, but the bet itself was very easy to find. I just punched "Cornell 7" into the search bar and found it pretty easily.

items.title: What’s Your Lamest Daydream?
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
Time for your weekly edition of the Defector Funbag. Got something on your mind? Today, we're talking about hockey, Jane Austen, Steven Spielberg, how to start dating, and more.

Drew is off this week, and I'm your substitute. I write about hockey, baseball, and a bunch of other stuff here at Defector. I also just published a book of essays about the movie , called , which I co-wrote with the amazing critic and novelist Emily St. James. It's a great gift for Christmas, but there is no greater gift than being able to answer your letters. So let's get to it.

items.title: Some Wins Feel More Like Losses
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Without knowing for sure whether this is actually true, we can still surmise that the Washington Commanders felt better about losing Monday night's game than they did about their delightfully grotesque tie against the Giants in Week 5. And we are almost certain the San Francisco 49ers felt worse in victory. Their record stayed spotless, but in making their escape, they caught a glimpse of the grim future that is in their front yard.

If you chose to avoid last night's Commanders–49ers game in the shadows of Hell's Substation, you are finding out today what happens when the scoreboard lies, and also when it becomes permissible to lie about the scoreboard. The practical truth is that the 49ers won 23-17, and remain one of the NFL's three undefeated teams. The victory broadened their lead in the NFC West to half the schedule—a margin of three games over the barely tenable Seattle Seahawks after six weeks of action. The math here is nearly unassailable, but hold on a moment while we assail it.

By losing, the Commanders managed not only to drop from 1-4-1, the fourth-worst record in the sport, but to complete a second consecutive week of winless football from the entire NFC East. Those divisional rivals pulled together to lose six games outright and tie a seventh in humiliating fashion. This is the first time an entire division has gone without a single team winning in back-to-back weeks since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, and almost certainly the first time ever, though we suspect nobody is bored enough to give that research a go. Only one team in the division, the New York Giants, has a winning record, and none of them have a positive point differential. After six weeks, the NFC East has fashioned itself as a hideous homage to the American League West, the new standard for no standards at all.

items.title: ‘Barbara Forever’ Won’t Let You Forget
items.author: Sohini Desai
items.content:
After listening to a critique of the Miss America pageant on a public radio station, Barbara Hammer declared herself a feminist. Then she left her husband. Then she became a lesbian. This was the early 1970s, and it wasn’t long before someone gifted baby gay Hammer a Super-8 and she commenced pointing it—lovingly, relentlessly—at every human crease and crevice in her life. Around this time, Hammer started writing down her name and address and placing them in balloons for others to find. “Otherwise I’d be lost in the world,” she said of the practice in an “exit interview,” given just before she died in 2019. 

Brydie O’Connor’s is one of these balloons: a documentary worthy of its iconic subject, that captures and arranges fragments of Barbara for us to turn over in our hands. It’s a devoted, sincere ode to the avant-garde artist, who, as she put it, made movies out of sex and life—more than 80 of them, to be a little more precise, over the course of half a century. Hammer filmed herself and her personal relationships obsessively, creating the vast archive that serves as the basis of . At the beginning of the film, there’s a series of images of Hammer pointing a camera into a passing window, or the rearview mirror of a car or motorcycle, her left eye squinting, her right looking into a viewfinder. We often see Barbara holding and speaking directly to the camera in the documentary, creating the uncanny sense that she made it herself, from beyond the grave. 

Though Hammer narrates the entire documentary, the narrative is pieced together from various sources. Barbara’s voice will sound effortful and aged at one moment, then youthful and mischievous in the next. O’Connor also replicates her subject’s love of a match cut, folding together images from throughout Hammer’s career. The result is not the chronology of a life, but the story of a filmmaker—starting when Barbara first picked up a camera, and ending with who she became to others. It’s a story of self-creation and self-plunder, of Barbara inventing herself and using her life as the raw material of her artistry.

items.title: I Love The Colorful Stars
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
A Weird Star is a classic place-setter in fiction. Put a Weird Star in the sky, even if it never has anything to do with the plot, and you know we're somewhere different and alien. Anything that's clearly not our Sun, and you're cooking with gas. Maybe it's a binary system, and there's two suns. Maybe it's large and looming. Maybe it's even flickering, like Jack Vance used, to excellent effect. But rarely do authors fuck around with color. A star is white, or red if it's going out soon, or, if the planet is question is truly fucked, the star is blue because that's the hottest color there is. Those are the colors of stars, we figured. Not even sci-fi authors could conceive of a mechanism to get some new tints in there.

As is often the case, the real universe turns out to be stranger than imagination. Stars, under the right circumstances, can appear to observers on their orbiting planets in a wide spectrum of colors, from hot pink to the green of cucumber lime Gatorade. "Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star," said Mark Hollands, an astrophysicist at the University of Warwick and lead author on the study. I'm imagining it, Mark! It rocks!

The paper, published last week in RAS Techniques and Instruments, doesn't rely on having found some new stars lit up like Christmas lights. Instead, it's a breakthrough in modeling. Traditionally, stars are modeled as putting out black-body radiation. Black bodies are mathematical conveniences, idealized objects: perfectly opaque and non-reflective, and emitting light in all wavelengths. Black bodies do not actually exist, but stars are close enough to that the models work for most purposes, which is the important thing. In black-body radiation, light will only ever vary depending on the temperature of the object, going from red to white to blue as the object gets hotter. Play around with the burners on your stove to grasp this immediately.

items.title: Rays Clinch Ultimate Thrifter World Series
items.author: Kathryn Xu
items.content:
For a moment there, it was getting a bit sleepy. In the bottom of the seventh inning, the Tampa Bay Rays were up 3-1 on the Cleveland Guardians: a lead, but not an insurmountable one. Each of their three runs came from plinking away at the Guardians' relievers—the Guardians were reduced to a bullpen game to fend off elimination—in the second and third innings. Then, up came Junior Caminero with a runner on. After that, it was impossible to drowse off.

The numbers on the home run themselves are not very impressive, nor was the timing particularly special. Caminero just dinked the foul pole; Statcast indicates that it would have only been a home run in Houston, New York, and, indeed, Tampa. Speaking purely in homer quality, it paled in comparison to his teammate Yandy Díaz's next-inning dagger. But absent the aesthetic appeal of a no-doubter, or the narrative sway of a game-winner, what made Caminero's home run incredible was Junior Caminero.

items.title: Sometimes A Team Just Wants To Hire A Famous Guy
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
The moment general manager Chris Ballard was given Fredo's kiss by the Indianapolis Colts' HR department Monday morning, the rumor mill started to churn up replacements. This is bleak work, but consider that the alternative was analyzing how the Colts managed to lose at home against a previously winless Titans team on Sunday. The first name on that list, per Dan Patrick, was Peyton Manning. It's a perfectly silly, superficial, and absolutely in-play choice for the job: the only person who does insurance commercials more often than Flo from Progressive.

That's because Manning is the preeminent former Indianapolis Colt, a quarterback who won a Super Bowl ring for the team and had the best seasons of his Hall of Fame career in that town. It's in play because Manning is an omnipresent medioid who ably plays the affable goober, but is in real life anything but. It's also in play because the Colts are owned by the daughter of the late Jim Irsay, Carlie Irsay-Gordon, an owner who takes notes on the sidelines in a constant quest to avoid just being seen as another fail-offspring in a league that's lousy with them. After the team's final loss of last season, she asked Ballard if he believed he still had "his juju." Given that he got canned with a career record in the job of 72-82-1 and the Colts haven't reached the playoffs since the 2020 season, it puts a serious strain on the concept of "juju."

Somewhere in that notebook, at some point during Sunday's grim and lifeless 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans, for god's sake, Irsay-Gordon presumably wrote "this juju sucks," if not in so many words then decisively enough to punch Ballard's ticket. Irsay-Gordon explained her sideline note-taking thusly two weeks ago to Front Office Sports:

items.title: World’s Most Normal Goalie: “The Past Is Dead, There’s Nothing For You There”
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
When last we checked in with Devin Cooley, he was serving as the backup goaltender for one of the worst teams in the league—I mean, downright putrid, couldn't-pay-me-to-watch bad. Not a lot has changed about the Calgary Flames in 11 months. They have two wins so far, second-fewest in the NHL. They have allowed 37 goals, second-most in the league. They're sporting a goal differential of minus-20 in just eight games played, which means that if you attend a Flames game, you should expect to see them lose by multiple goals. In practice they have lost multiple games by four, and multiple games by five.

It takes a type to thrive in that environment, and Cooley might be that type. All goalies are strange—they are under constant, ego-deforming pressure, and must spend an unhelpful amount of time alone in their own minds—but Cooley is rare in being able to describe his specific flavor of strange. In that interview last year, he displayed a mindset that, while nihilist on its face, is probably pretty healthy in its ability to compartmentalize each save, each game, and wall it off from the saves and games he has yet to face. "Nothing matters," he said, "nobody cares, we're all going to die."

So what would the Flames' poor 2026 start do for Cooley's mood? Well, ah, at least his bunny Tito seems in good spirits. Good for Tito. He's the only living being who can attend a Flames game and not suffer psychic damage.

items.title: How Did A Famous, Lying UFC Vet Get Shot Conducting Shadowy Paramilitary Operations In The Congo?
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
On Oct. 9, the reported that UFC veteran Tim Kennedy was recovering in the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center after he'd been shot three times while conducting a deadly, murkily defined operation with Erik Prince's private military group, in the remote highlands of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwandan-backed rebel group M23. The constellation of proper nouns in that sentence is staggering, and lights the way to understanding the strange, idiosyncratic state of affairs in one of the most mineral-rich areas of the planet. I am going to walk you through this story, proper noun by proper noun (out of order), in hopes of untangling the messy web.

Democratic Republic of Congo

A few billion years ago, the large-scale geologic province known as the Congo Craton formed. Cratons are geologic provinces that have survived the endless churn of tectonic activity that recycles most of the Earth's crust, meaning they contain some of the most ancient rocks on the planet. In central Africa, the Congo Craton is overlaid by the massive and comparatively young Congo Basin, a sedimentary complex that contains the largest deposit of cobalt in the world, in addition to huge amounts of copper, gold, tantalum, and other valuable minerals.

items.title: Tiny Flame Of Joy Extinguished In Sacramento
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
Where the Sacramento Kings are concerned, all "joy" is relative. But this team, which projects to be among the NBA's worst, enjoyed one charming preseason storyline: the apparent revival of Ben Simmons as an actual rotation player. The basketball gods have chosen to deprive them and their fans of even this meager comfort. ESPN's Shams Charania reported on Sunday that Simmons tore his right Achilles tendon during a Kings practice, ending his season before it really began.

Simmons, a former All-NBA selection, went completely unsigned during the 2025-26 season. He deliberately distanced himself from basketball during that time, not even watching a game until the playoffs. That distance allowed the 30-year-old to pursue a maritime passion—sport fishing—and also allowed him to rebuild himself into a player good enough to sign the veteran minimum for a team projected by ESPN to win 21.7 games.

"I didn't touch a ball for the whole year," Simmons told reporters at Kings media day. "I didn't watch basketball. I just focused on getting my body right and my mind right." Multiple back surgeries had siphoned away his former athleticism. But Simmons observed a "night and day" difference in his mental health, after allowing his back to heal in his year off; affirmed his love of the sport; and, when asked if he could get back to his old self, said: "He's there. He woke up."

items.title: It Took A Lot Of Underachieving To Get Miami At No. 1
items.author: Israel Daramola
items.content:
College football had its first Blood Week of the season. This weekend saw losses for eight ranked teams, and even the teams that didn't lose had extremely close calls. That brings us to the Miami Hurricanes, who played a big rivalry game with unranked Florida State, which turned into a shootout even though Miami is supposed to have a championship defense and Florida State is Florida State.

After four quarters and two overtimes, Miami beat FSU, 43-35. Saturday's victory came only after two seemingly successful Hail Marys by FSU quarterback Ashton Daniels were consecutively called back. The first was due to a holding penalty on the offense. The second attempt looked like it ended with FSU receiver Duce Robinson having dual possession of the ball, but it was ultimately ruled an interception for Miami.

items.title: Jalen Hurts Is Out For The Season, And The Eagles Have A Lot Of Questions To Answer [Update]
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
Jalen Hurts's season is over. On Monday, his agent Nicole Lynn, in conjunction with the Philadelphia Eagles, released a statement about the quarterback's health situation as it pertains to the blood clot in his leg, an issue that was first revealed publicly on Oct. 15 and which landed Hurts on injured reserve two days later.

Monday's statement sheds more light on what exactly happened since the Eagles' trip to London to face the Jacksonville Jaguars on Oct. 11. The relevant part is also the scariest part:

items.title: Rolling Snakes Reinvent The Wheel
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
For eons, roly-polies have rightfully dominated the rolling space, at least in our imagination. The crustaceans' astonishing ability to transform from a legged arthropod into a perfect sphere, a behavior called volvation, earned the bugs their nickname. But the bugs are far from the only rollers in the animal kingdom. Pangolins, hedgehogs, echidnas, and armadillos do it too, curling up their bodies into defensive balls. So does the Venezuelan pebble toad, which tucks in its head and tumbles down slopes to escape tarantulas. The Mount Lyell salamander rolls too, coiling itself into a wheel and bouncing down steep rocks. None of these animals become quite as Platonic a sphere as the roly-poly, but they do well enough.

But becoming a ball is not the only way to roll. The dwarf reed snake has found another way to roll away from danger, not by becoming a ball but by becoming something like a hoop. This peculiar motion, the mechanics of which are analyzed in a new paper in raises an important question: What is more sinister, a snake slithering in the grass or a snake rolling itself like a possessed wheel?

items.title: Nobody’s Having More Fun Than Sebastian Fundora
items.author: Dave McKenna
items.content:
Call it a buzzer beating. The reigning WBC super welterweight champ and most interesting man in boxing, Sebastian Fundora, delivered as interesting a knockout as memory serves while retaining his title Saturday night in Las Vegas. 

Fundora, the tallest 154-pound champ in history (6-foot-5.5 inches) and someone who taunts opponents about the ease with which he makes weight, wounded pesky challenger Ermal Hadribeaj with a vicious assortment of body blows and haymakers to the head as the last seconds of the last round of their brutal and surprisingly competitive 12-round slugfest ticked away. Then, just as the final bell sounded, Fundora landed a lightning-fast kill shot to Hadribeaj’s chin. Referee Thomas Taylor began counting out Hadribeaj, who was sprawled on the canvas, as most onlookers inside the casino arena were wondering what was going on, given that the clock had run out. 

But, no matter what the title of that ubiquitous '80s and ‘90s sitcom implies, you can no longer actually be saved by the bell in boxing, not even the bell ending the last round. Even though Hadribeaj got to his feet just before getting a 10 count, Taylor ruled he was in no condition to continue. Utilizing the powers vested in him by the so-called Unified Rules of Boxing, a package of uniform edicts which since around the turn of the century have been adopted in Nevada and throughout the U.S. that allows for fights to be stopped even after the final bell under such circumstances, Taylor waved his hands over his head and declared a knockout. (Decorated vets Terence Crawford and Tim Bradley, who sat ringside as working media for the TV broadcast, vented at Taylor after the fight for not letting Hadribeaj go home with a decision loss.)

items.title: There’s A Difference Between Honoring A Dead Artist And Exploiting One
items.author: Dave McKenna
items.content:
Another new album of old Eva Cassidy recordings, called , is about to come out. Cassidy, a peerless D.C. songbird, died 30 years ago next month. Her supply of unheard material ran out long ago. Those who legally control Cassidy's songbook transitioned from merely curating her art, as her label still claims to be doing with the latest project, to altering it. gave me the blues.

Cassidy's talent was rare and huge, though it took her dying to get the music industry to notice. And the story of her quiet, relatively anonymous life giving way to massive posthumous popularity the world over is equally amazing. When she was alive and singing, Cassidy was unknown outside the D.C. area, where she was born and raised and stayed until the end. She really wasn't a big draw in her hometown, either. She had a small, hardcore group of local fans who loved her for her pitch-perfect voice and multi-genre musical range, and also for being a serene, sweet soul seemingly as oblivious to her own artistic genius as were all the record-label honchos who rejected her when she was knocking on doors looking for a deal. She paid her bills by working at a plant nursery, not by making beautiful music. Cassidy and her band gigged mostly at bars, never at theaters or music halls. She financed her own recordings, including 1996's , the only solo album she lived to see released. 

But right when that record was about to come out, Cassidy began telling friends she wasn't feeling right, and died from melanoma mere months later. Some Cassidy recordings got into the hands of pop influencers in England in the late 1990s, most notably her cover of "Over the Rainbow," and over the next few years she became a phenomenon throughout Europe and then the world. Another big break came when Team USA's Michelle Kwan skated to Cassidy's version of "Fields of Gold" on the way to a bronze medal during the 2002 Olympics.

items.title: Jaguars Junction: Week 6
items.author: Hamilton Nolan
items.content:
Last week, when the Jacksonville Jaguars played the Philadelphia Eagles in London U.K., I devised a typically great "bit." My idea was to write a piece casting Philadelphians as clumsy oafs, juxtaposed with Jacksonvilleans, who would be portrayed as urbane sophisticates. The essay was to start with a dramatic scene of a Philadelphia resident in London, behaving as the proverbial bull in a China shop, demanding: 

"DUHH ... ME WANT MEAT SANDWICH!" 

As the poor Pennsylvanian proved himself a rube, the Jacksonville resident, dressed in a rakish Savile Row suit, would shrug apologetically and, with a smattering of cosmopolitan remarks, assure his London host that not all Americans are so painfully uncultured. As the Jacksonville man, pausing only to refill his pipe, won over the room with a series of digressions on the legacy of the East India Company, wandering Philadelphians would periodically interject:

items.title: Good Art Is Worth Waiting For
items.author: Kelsey McKinney
items.content:
This article contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.

About halfway into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s new A24 movie , there is a scene that plays like a memory. Nathan Fielder stands, in the present of the movie, inside a San Diego ocean-front house looking out at the crashing waves, remembering. Then, playing for the viewer: two unidentifiable people in the ocean, frolicking, swimming in the icy cold waves, a blonde woman and a brunette man, both tall, both smiling. The camaraderie between them is undeniable.
